content_metadata.description: Wayne Scott delivers a talk at Ignite Portland, focusing on the challenges of social work, specifically vicarious trauma, and the need for appreciation and gratitude towards social workers.

qAndA.answer: The image highlights the unrealistic expectation for social workers to constantly be resilient without addressing their own needs for self-care, leading to burnout and compassion fatigue.
qAndA.question: What does the image of Superman represent in the context of Wayne Scott's talk?

qAndA.answer: Wayne Scott recounts an anecdote about encountering a homeless man asking for money and admits to ignoring him, which he considers complicit in social injustice.
qAndA.question: What specific example does Wayne Scott use to illustrate how easy it is to become complicit in social injustice?

qAndA.answer: Mirror neurons, which fire both when we perform an action and when we observe someone else doing the same, allow us to 'feel what they feel' during trauma narratives.
qAndA.question: What is the scientific basis for the emotional impact of listening to someone's story of trauma, according to Wayne Scott?

qAndA.answer: He suggests giving social workers practical gifts like dark chocolate, a gift card, or a raise to acknowledge their low pay and valuable work.
qAndA.question: What concrete suggestion does Wayne Scott offer as a way to celebrate World Social Work Day?

qAndA.answer: He draws a parallel between the sacrifice of soldiers and social workers, suggesting that both deserve recognition and gratitude for their service.
qAndA.question: How does Wayne Scott connect the concept of thanking veterans for their service to his proposal of thanking social workers?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hi.
My name is Wayne.
Hi, everyone.
I've been a social worker for over 20 years.
I've worked in a psychiatric hospital, drop-in center for people with mental illness,
and a therapeutic community for men who struggled with criminal conduct and substance abuse,
and that was a really fun job.
I'm also a writer.
I like to read stories and write stories.
As soon as I became a social worker, I realized that social work is about listening to stories.
So what I want to talk about tonight is a hazard that affects people who do social work,
psychotherapy, counseling, all the professions that work with people who are in crisis.
It's called Vicarious Trauma.
But before I tell you about that, I want to tell you about the first last great book that
I read.
It was a memoir by Eve Ensler, who's a playwright and an activist.
She talked about going to the Congo and talking with and listening to girls and women talk
about their experiences.
These were women who were brutalized by atrocities.
Atrocities, we can't even imagine.
When a survivor talks about an injustice or a suffering that happened to her, we become
part of the story.
When a survivor feels hurt, she's able to take the story to a new place, often a more
hopeful place.
Listening in this very present way that I'm talking about is actually an act of social
justice.
I know that that sounds kind of weird.
Social justice is supposed to be about redistributing income or overthrowing desks or everybody
getting health care.
But there's an intangible side to it as well.
When I go to the grocery store, I will often notice a man with a sign who looks really
tired and hungry.
And even though I think of myself as a really nice guy, when I'm rushing to get my own groceries,
I will often not make eye contact with him.
I rush right by and I become part of the problem.
Any social worker will tell you that it's not easy to pay attention.
If you want to understand that this whole syndrome of Vicarious Trauma better and you don't
do this kind of work, all you have to do is remember how you felt when you heard about
the massacre at Sandy Hook Elementary School.
You weren't physically there, but you kind of were.
Brain scientists have discovered these things called mirror neurons.
When I listen to someone talk about an experience of injustice or suffering, mirror neurons fire
in my brain in the same area where suffering occurs.
I feel what they feel.
Now empathy is great.
Our intelligence as a species is a social intelligence.
We stay connected to survive.
But imagine those mirror neurons firing in your head in the same place where suffering
happens all day long.
Social workers talk about compassion fatigue and listening to the stories can make you
feel numb and empty and hopeless.
Then there's this hormone called cortisol, which is great if you're in an emergency and
you need a superhuman burst of strength.
But if you live in a constant state of emergency because you work with people in crisis, then
your body is bathed in cortisol.
It affects your sleep and your appetite.
It can make you jittery and it can make you fat.
What I do these days is I go around to agencies talking with them about Vicarious Trauma.
And I'll be honest with you, I do meet some social workers who are kind of jaded, kind
of cynical, kind of burnt out and kind of exhausted.
These are folks who need a vacation, a career counselor, or maybe a job as a barista.
But more often, I meet extraordinary people, wholehearted people who are living from a
deep sense of purpose, folks who have figured out exceptional ways of taking care of themselves.
And it never ceases to amaze me.
No matter in spite of all the hardships of doing this work, people still choose to do
it.
A while back, I heard about this event called World Social Work Day.
And I'm embarrassed to admit this, but I got a little bit excited.
One of the drawbacks of being a white middle class guy is that we crave attention.
We wash a dish and then we wait for the applause.
So World Social Work Day came and it went.
There were some speeches somewhere by somebody.
There was some talk about vision, but what I really wanted was some dark chocolate, a gift
card to pals, or maybe a race.
But I don't think any of that's going to happen.
I have a different idea.
When I was growing up and I met a veteran, I was told to say thank you for your service.
And even though I never agree with the reasons we go to war, when I meet a soldier, I am all
struck by the sacrifice they make, I put politics aside and I say thank you for your service.
As World Social Work Day rounds the corner again, I want to make a suggestion that we thank
those people who make a choice to do social justice work.
It doesn't pay a lot.
It isn't glamorous and the hazards are great.
It's a post-industrial, capitalistic world that doesn't make a place for everybody at the
table.
It helps to correct a deep imbalance.
So I want to start this tradition by saying to my family, my friends, my neighbors, my
colleagues, and my students who brave the hazards of Icaria's trauma to do social justice work.
Thank you for your service.

youtube_description: If you had five minutes on stage what would you say? What if you only got 20 slides and they rotated automatically after 15 seconds? Around the world geeks have been putting together Ignite nights to show their answers. With our 12th session of Ignite Portland here are the speakers and their wonderful presentations at the Hollywood Theater held on Thursday November 14th, 2013, in Portland, Oregon. Video production by brytCAST - http://brytcast.com
